transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it’s mostly that I keep checking things—little things, really. Boxes, lists I’ve made, drawers in the condo. I’ll look once, and then somehow I’m back there looking again, even though I know I already did it.

My wife will be standing by the door waiting, you know, and I tell myself, “Just leave it be,” but I can’t quite move on until I check again. It’s a bit embarrassing. We’ve lived in that condo a long time—nice place, though the drawers are a little shallow, whoever designed those kitchens didn’t think much about storage—but anyway, yes, that’s what brought me in. I’m spending too much time going back over the same things.
Do you find that you have certain thoughts or worries that come up when you're checking these things—like a fear that something bad might happen if you don't check them again?

Yes, I suppose there is a worry behind it. It’s not so much that the house will burn down or anything dramatic like that. It’s more this nagging thought that I might’ve thrown away something important from my old teaching files, or put some tool in the wrong box.

I’ll tell myself, “Oh, come on, that’s unlikely,” but then it comes back. Those old files, you know, some of them I kept from when I was teaching, and you never know when you’ll want a handout or a note—though I’m not even working now, so it’s silly. But the thought sticks there, and I have trouble settling until I check again.
Do these nagging thoughts feel different from your usual worries, like they come into your mind automatically and are difficult to control, even if you try to push them away?

Yes, that’s about right. They sort of pop back in on their own, even after I’ve decided it’s probably nothing. I’ll think, “No, I didn’t throw out anything important,” or “That tool is in the right box,” and then a minute later the same little doubt is there again.

It’s funny, those teaching files—I kept so many of them, probably more than anyone needs. My wife used to say the condo was turning into a records room. But yes, the point is, even when I try to push the thought aside, it doesn’t stay aside very well. It makes me feel unsettled until I go and check.
When you go back to check those things, does it feel like something bad will happen if you don’t, or does it help reduce a feeling of anxiety that builds up when you try to resist checking?

It’s more that I can’t move on until I do it, if that makes sense. I don’t always have some big disaster in mind. I just get this feeling like, “Wait, did I really check that box? Did I look in that drawer?” And then there I am, going back over the same boxes, the same lists, the condo drawers.

My wife will be waiting by the door, and I know perfectly well I already looked. I even remember looking, sometimes. But until I check again, it sort of sits there and nags at me. Then after I check, I feel a little more able to leave it alone—at least for the moment. Those drawers, by the way, they never did fit things properly, but yes, it’s the checking that’s the problem.
Do these thoughts ever come up completely unbidden, like out of nowhere, and feel unpleasant or unwanted, rather than just being a normal concern you can easily let go of?

Yes, they do feel unwanted. It’s not like I sit down and decide to worry about the old files or the tools. I’ll be doing something else, or trying to get ready to leave, and suddenly I’ll think, “What if I threw away that one important handout?” or “Did I put that tool in the wrong box?”

And I know, logically, it’s probably fine. I mean, some of those teaching papers are years old—half of them I probably don’t need anyway, though you never know, I suppose. But the thought just comes back on its own and makes me uneasy. It’s hard to settle until I’ve checked.

Have these thoughts and the checking behaviors started to take up a lot of your time—like more than an hour a day—or have they begun to interfere with your daily life, your work, or your relationships in any significant way?

It has gotten in the way, yes. I don’t know that I’ve sat with a stopwatch and added it up, but the condo unpacking has taken far longer than it should have. I’ll open a box, check what’s in it, then somehow I’m back checking it again instead of just putting things away.

And because of that, I’ve been putting off other things. I do some library tutoring preparation, and I keep telling myself I’ll get to it once I’m sure everything is sorted properly. Same with hobbies—little things I used to just sit down and do. Instead I feel like I can’t quite move on until I’ve verified things enough.

It sounds silly when I say it, because it’s only boxes and drawers, but it does eat into the day.
Have you noticed these thoughts and checking behaviors happening even when you’re not particularly stressed or worried about other things in your life?

Yes, I think so. It isn’t only when I’m upset about something else. What brought me in is really that I’ll be in the middle of ordinary things—trying to finish unpacking, or get out the door—and I find myself checking the same boxes, the same lists, those condo drawers, over and over before I can move on.

And the odd thing is, I know I already looked. Sometimes my wife is standing there waiting for me to just leave it be, and I’m thinking, “Yes, yes, I checked that,” but then I still go back and look again. It’s not always tied to some big stressful event. It just sort of catches me.

When you have these intrusive thoughts, do you feel driven to perform certain behaviors or mental acts—like checking, counting, or repeating words—to reduce the anxiety or prevent something bad from happening?

Yes, mostly it’s checking. I don’t really do counting or saying words, not that I’ve noticed. But when that thought hits me, I feel like I have to go back and look.

It’s the same boxes, the lists, the drawers in the condo. I’ll know perfectly well I already checked—sometimes I can practically picture myself doing it—and my wife will be waiting there, wanting me to just leave it alone. But I still feel pulled to open it again before I can move on.

It reminds me a bit of when I used to organize papers for teaching, you know, you’d think you’d put the handout in the right folder and then—well, anyway, that’s the sort of feeling. Like I can’t quite trust it until I check one more time.

When these thoughts about throwing away something important or misplacing a tool come up, do they cause you a lot of inner distress, and do you feel that by checking again, you're somehow preventing something bad from happening or making the thoughts go away?

Yes, it does bother me inside, though I don’t know if I’d call it panic exactly. It’s more that I get stuck on it. I’ll think, “What if I put that in the wrong box?” or “What if I need that later and can’t find it?” and then I’m back opening the same box or looking in the same drawer.

The thing is, I know I already looked. I can remember looking. My wife will be standing there waiting for me to just leave it alone, and I’ll still feel like I can’t quite move on until I check it again. It’s not very sensible, I know. It’s just boxes, lists, the condo drawers—well, when we moved, we had so many of those little odds and ends, screws and chargers and who knows what, and you think you’ll remember where you put them, but then—

Anyway, yes, checking again sort of settles the thought for the moment. Or at least I’m hoping it will. Then sometimes it doesn’t last very long.
